Android from the foundation · Puzzle 5 of 6

Binder is the post office between processes

Processes can't touch each other's memory, so every call between them is packed into bytes and carried by the kernel's Binder driver, stamped with the caller's identity.

The problem

Your app (one process) needs system_server (another process) to start a screen. But processes can't touch each other's memory: that was the whole point of the sandbox. So how does a method call get from one to the other?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Binder is a driver inside the Linux kernel (drivers/android/binderThe Binder driver in mainline Linux (now written in Rust) stamps the sender's user ID on every transaction. Android phones run Android's own kernel branches, which may still use the older C driver. 392 from_parent, 393 sender_euid: Kuid::current_euid(),transaction.rs, line 392 · Linux kernel ↗). The kernel is the only code allowed to touch every process's memory, so it can carry messages across. Your side holds a proxy; the other side has a stub that calls the real object. Arguments travel as a ParcelThe flat byte buffer that carries arguments across processes. 237 public final class Parcel {Parcel.java, line 237 · AOSP frameworks/base ↗.

Two facts that come up all the time:

  • Who's calling: Binder stamps every call with the caller's UID and PID. The receiver reads it with Binder.getCallingUid()Native: the UID the kernel stamped on the call. The caller can't fake it. 338 public static final native int getCallingUid();Binder.java, line 338 · AOSP frameworks/base ↗ to check permissions.
  • Size limit: the transaction buffer is about 1 MB per process, shared by all transactions in progress.

The analogy

A TV remote. You press a button on the remote (the proxy); the TV (the real object) is in another room. The post office (Binder) carries the envelope, and stamps the sender's address on it.

You put a 3 MB bitmap into an Intent extra and start an Activity. What happens?

Right. The Intent travels over Binder, whose buffer is about 1 MB per process, shared by all calls in flight. Pass a file URI or an ID instead.

Not quite. Step back through the diagram above, then try again.

Can an app lie to a system service about who it is?

Right. The UID comes from the kernel, not from the data, so the receiver can trust it for permission checks.

Not quite. Step back through the diagram above, then try again.

On which thread does a Binder call arrive in the receiving process?

Right. Binder threads receive calls; to touch the UI, they post a message to the main thread.

What you now know

proxy → Parcel → kernel (Binder) → Binder thread → stub → real method, and back. Every Intent, every startActivity(), every system service call travels this way, with a buffer of about 1 MB.
